October 2026 · Read with the Diagnosis Report

The build plan

Phase 1 took your business apart. This plan puts it back together.

Phase 1 was the hard part to hear. We showed you where the money leaks, where the work breaks, and why all of it runs through you. This is the part you've been waiting for: every fix, in the order it has to happen, with who does it, the week it happens, and the test that proves it's done.

Nothing in here asks you to work harder. Most of it takes work off you. The goal is a business that tells you the truth about its money every Monday, carries itself through the winter, and runs for a week without you. Three times, tested, before Day 180.

What revenue per dollar of pay means

It's what the business brings in for every dollar it pays its people: crews, subcontractors, office, sales and management, all of it. From September 2024 to August 2025, every dollar of pay brought in $2.76. From September 2025 to September 2026, it brought in $2.24. Fifty-two cents sounds small. It isn't. Over those last twelve months the business took in $2,574,007 and paid $1,149,049 to do it. At the earlier rate, the same revenue needed $934,288 of pay. The difference is $214,761 a year, about a fifth of gross profit, what the business keeps after the direct cost of doing the work. That money went to pay that grew faster than the work it paid for. Getting back to $2.76 puts that money back.

You already built more than you think

Most of this plan switches on things you already paid for and never got to use.

A leadership team

A GM running operations, a head project manager, a field supervisor and a financial coordinator. The seats exist. What's missing is a system that lets them decide without calling you.

A repeat book

82% of your 2025 visits ran on recurring routes. Customers come back. The routes just expire under them.

A full written system

17 procedures, dated January 2026, with named checklists and message templates: lead intake, sales, scheduling, billing, retention, maintenance, installs, safety, equipment, onboarding. Writing them is the slow part of a delivery system, and it's done. They're switched off.

A source that works

Google-sourced customers, paid and organic together, brought in about $6.56 for every dollar of Google ads in 2025. Billboards got more than three times as much: $120,092 against $35,553 for Google.

A team already moving

Nicole sets route order every week now and runs a weekly rework report. Both stay. The build makes them easier, not different.

None of this gets thrown out. The build wires it together so you stop being the wiring.

Eight pieces, in the order that holds

You'll want to start with leads. Every owner does, because “I need more work” is how the problem feels from the inside. Leads go last on purpose. More work poured into a business that can't cost it, staff it or bank it makes your week worse and charges you for the privilege.

So each piece either feeds the next one real numbers or protects it from bad ones. One change from the usual order: the money goes in early. Last winter, November through February, $487,249 of revenue came in and $502,608 went out, owner draws and loan payments included, and the account hit $4,297 in December. This winter lands in the middle of the build. So the accounts open during Phase 2 and the money rules switch on in the first week of Phase 3, before the slow months bite.

Six things that happen first

These stop damage that's permanent or expensive to undo, so they run in the first days of Phase 2, before the design work. None needs a design session.

The full step

Line staff lose the delete button on jobs, quotes, visits and invoices, and archive instead. 1,050 records were deleted between July 1 and September 16, and deleted records don't come back. True duplicates still get deleted, by one named person.

Step by step
  1. Pull the user list and mark every line staff login.
  2. Remove delete on jobs, quotes, visits and invoices for those roles. Leave archive on.
  3. Name the one person allowed to delete a true duplicate, and write that down.
  4. Tell the office the rule in one line: archive, never delete.
  5. Check the delete log each Monday until it reads zero for four weeks.
The full step

In the September 15 report, 130 of your 231 routes were set to end before the rebuild reaches them in late November. 92 end in the last week of October alone, 47 of them Applegreen's, and 10 had already passed their end date by early October. First test the winter setup on one route: visits paused for the off-season, or a winter schedule. Then extend every route ending before the rebuild to 99 years, the way the routing report showed. Any that already ran out get rebuilt first. Otherwise every one of them gets rebuilt by hand in the spring.

Step by step
  1. Pick one route and test the winter setup: visits paused for the off-season, or a winter schedule.
  2. Check the test route still shows the right spring start and doesn't bill in winter.
  3. Extend every route ending before the rebuild to a 99-year length, the 92 October routes first.
  4. Rebuild the 10 that already passed their end date before anything else.
  5. Spot-check 10 extended routes the next week for correct visits and billing.
The full step

Pull ten of the invoices behind the $78,683 and match each to the bank. If they were paid outside Jobber, the balance is a records problem. If they weren't, it's money owed, and the collection steps in 6.1 run on it. Until that test runs, nobody calls it money.

Step by step
  1. Pick ten of the 84, largest first, across different customers.
  2. For each, search the bank for a matching payment by amount, name and date.
  3. Mark each one paid outside Jobber, partly paid, or unpaid.
  4. If most were paid, clean the records and fix the step that left them open.
  5. If they weren't, the collection steps in 6.1 run on the balance.
The full step

You have the itemized list of every Zelle in 2025 and 2026. Mark each line as your pay, a vendor, or a business cost you covered personally. Your CPA needs it before anything in the money system can be set.

Step by step
  1. Open the itemized Zelle list for 2025 and 2026.
  2. Mark each line as owner pay, a vendor, or a business cost paid personally.
  3. Flag anything nobody recognizes for David.
  4. David confirms the marks.
  5. Send the sorted list to the CPA with the step 2.2 numbers.
The full step

One person who'll set the floor, the tax rate and your draw. Nothing in piece 2 moves without them.

Step by step
  1. Confirm who the accountant is now.
  2. Confirm they'll set the floor, the tax set-aside, the reserve and your draw.
  3. Share their contact so the step 2.2 meeting can be booked.
The full step

OpFix access to FingerCheck, and the tier pricing sheet Nicole prices from. Both feed the catalog and the labor costing.

  3. Confirm both are open by Oct 14.
Piece 1 of 8 · The operating hub · Phase 3, Nov 2 to Dec 6

Jobber starts telling the truth

Jobber gets your revenue right and your margin wrong, because nobody ever loaded what things cost.

Where it stands

78 of the 283 items in your catalog carry a $0 cost, including 71 of your 139 services. This year, 141 of the 291 line names on your invoices aren't in the catalog at all. Somebody typed them in: $227,799 of work priced outside the catalog. Of 3,226 one-off jobs, 141 carry any labor cost. 88% of visits show zero tracked time. And every one of your 231 routes has an end date.

Labor cost goes in first

The full step

Each crew member, field and office, gets a labor cost in Jobber taken from ADP: wage plus payroll taxes. Jobber only applies labor cost to time logged after the rate exists, so every week this waits is a week of jobs at zero labor. Nothing else in the hub goes live until it's done.

Step by step
  1. Pull each person's wage from ADP, field and office.
  2. Add payroll taxes to get the loaded hourly cost per person.
  3. Enter each cost on that person in Jobber.
  4. Log a test visit and confirm the labor cost shows on the job.
  5. Nothing else in the hub goes live until this is done.
The full step

Every crew member gets their own Jobber login, and the shared crew accounts retire. The crew starts the timer on arrival and stops it on the way out. The target is 90% of visits with time on them, four weeks running. Below that, capacity can't be measured and paid demand can't turn on. Jobber prices plans by user count, so the added logins get checked against your plan in the design session.

Step by step
  1. Check the Jobber plan's user count and price the added logins.
  2. Create one login for every crew member. Retire the shared crew accounts.
  3. Show each crew lead how to start the timer on arrival and stop it leaving.
  4. Every Monday, Nicole reads tracked time by crew and follows up on gaps.
  5. Hit 90% by Nov 29, then hold it four straight weeks.
The full step

FingerCheck takes its hours from the Jobber timers, so a crew's day gets entered once, and FingerCheck departments match the trucks. Whether it reads Jobber directly or through a connector gets settled once we're inside FingerCheck.

Step by step
  1. Confirm inside FingerCheck whether it reads Jobber directly or needs a connector.
  2. Set FingerCheck departments to match the trucks.
  3. Run one pay period from timer hours side by side with the old way.
  4. Switch over once the two match.
Piece 1 of 8 · The operating hub · Phase 3, Nov 2 to Dec 6

Jobber starts telling the truth continued

A cost on everything you sell

The full step

All 283 items get their supplier cost and labor minutes, the 78 at $0 first. Your markup, about 3.5 to 4.5 times material cost today, lives in Nicole's head. It gets written into the catalog as a rule, and the tier pricing sheet goes in with it. The catalog cost is what you quote from and what a job is expected to cost.

Step by step
  1. List all 283 items, the 78 at $0 first.
  2. Add supplier cost from current invoices for every material item.
  3. Add labor minutes for every service, from timed visits where they exist.
  4. Write the markup rule, about 3.5 to 4.5 times material cost, into the catalog.
  5. Load the tier pricing sheet. Steve signs off costs, Nicole the pricing rule.
The full step

Each of the 141 off-catalog names maps to a catalog item or retires. Quotes get built from the catalog. A typed-in line shows up on the Monday report, so it gets fixed the same week.

Step by step
  1. List the 141 off-catalog names with their totals.
  2. Map each to a catalog item, or retire it.
  3. Add any real service that's missing to the catalog, with its cost.
  4. Turn on the Monday report line for typed-in lines.
  5. Fix each one the week it shows up.
The full step

105 jobs carry both a line-item material cost and a Bill.com expense for the same material, and only 10 of them land within 10% of each other. We check a sample against the receipts, and the sample settles the rule. The starting rule: the Bill.com expense is what the material actually cost, so on a job it replaces the catalog's material cost instead of adding to it. Expected against actual is the margin check. Until it's settled, no margin by job goes on any report.

Step by step
  1. Pull a sample of the 105 jobs.
  2. Check each against its receipts in Bill.com.
  3. Confirm the rule from the sample: the Bill.com expense replaces the catalog's material cost on the job.
  4. Set expected cost (catalog) against actual cost (Bill.com) as the margin check.
  5. No margin by job goes on any report until the rule is live.

Routes that run until the customer says stop

The full step

In the September 15 report, 144 of your 231 routes ended by December 31. Step 0.2 saves the first ones. This step sets every remaining route to a 99-year length. To change a route you edit it. A renewed annual agreement keeps the same route. A route closes only when the customer cancels.

Piece 3 of 8 · The delivery system · Phase 3, Nov 16 to Dec 13

Your 17 procedures leave the folder

Where it stands

Your checklists already exist in Jobber, with auto-attach switched off. In 13 months they were filled out 97 times, on 19 jobs, and 16 of those were customer jobs out of 3,457. So when something goes sideways, the fastest way to an answer is your phone. Four of the 17 procedures still have open questions written into them, like “behind schedule by more than ___.”

The fix isn't more writing. It's putting each procedure inside the step where the work happens, so following it is the easy way to do the job.

Piece 5 of 8 · Demand capture · Phase 3, Nov 23 to Dec 27

Every lead gets worked until it's decided

Where it stands

Your lead source list has 35 values. Ten are people's names, five are Facebook ad ID numbers, and “Vehicle Wrap” shows up twice with two spellings. 4,923 of your 7,017 clients have no source at all, and neither do 389 of the 1,418 new clients this year. 1,657 of the 1,674 requests this year came through one form, the residential online request, so the form can't tell you the channel. Tracking links show up on 13 clients, 12 of them from Facebook and Instagram ads. Google ads carry none. And 385 requests this year were archived with no quote and no reason Jobber can count.

That's why nobody can say what the ad spend returns. “Google” as a source holds people who clicked a search ad and people who found you on their own. Until paid and organic are split, that's a strong signal and not yet proof.

When they pass, spend moves toward your own ceiling of 8 to 10%, and toward what the tracking proves returns, at a known cost per booked job. Billboards wait until the reserve is funded. They aren't wrong forever, just wrong for now. Google Local Services Ads get a test against your search ads on the same tracking: you pay per lead, and the cost per booked job decides whether they stay. You make the spend call at the first Monday review after all four pass.

The cautious version

Bringing advertising to 10% of revenue on its own, a decision you'd already started, moves 2025's operating profit from $160,641 to about $248,000.

What Day 180 looks like

Same business, rebuilt. To keep it honest we held revenue and service mix exactly where 2025 left them, with no growth assumed. Two things change. Advertising sits at your own 10% ceiling, and pay comes back to the rate it ran at a year earlier. From September 2024 to August 2025, each dollar of pay brought in $2.76. From September 2025 to September 2026, it brought in $2.24. Closing that gap means 19% less pay for the same work, so the model takes 2025's pay down 19%.

David

A two-hour design session in Phase 2, your sign-off at each gate, two weeks of the call log, your CPA's time, and approval on the decision rules and the source list. From Phase 3 on, mostly reading the Monday report.

Nicole

Steve, Sean and Alejandro

You could run this without us

This is the how, and we're handing it to you on purpose. Every step, every owner, every date. You could give it to Nicole tomorrow and run it yourselves.

Here's what the record says about that. McKinsey's global surveys of large company change efforts put the success rate under 30%, and those efforts had teams and budgets behind them. The plan isn't the hard part. Holding it in place while the phones ring and the season runs is.

How to read this chart

Each line is money the business gets back, added up month by month for two years. What it gets back is the gap between the $160,641 of operating profit it made in 2025 and the $422,665 Day 180 target: $262,024 a year.

The gold line is building it with us. The gap closes over the first six months, and from Day 180 on the full amount comes back every month. After two years that adds up to $469,460.

The blue line is the same plan run alone. It closes the gap at the rate most change efforts succeed, under 3 in 10. After two years that adds up to $140,838.

The red line is changing nothing. Nothing comes back, and the same leaks keep running.

The space between gold and blue is $328,622 over two years. That's the cost of going it alone. Day 180 is a target, not a promise, and the gold line assumes it's hit.

If you'd rather run it yourselves, use it. It's yours either way, and we'd rather you use it than file it.

What happens next

Read it. Push back on anything that doesn't fit how your business actually runs, and we change it. If you go ahead, Phase 2 opens with the design session in the first week, and you approve every piece before it's built.

The business already makes the money. Now it gets a system that keeps it.
